utility.notes: City Utilities is a municipally-owned utility serving Springfield, Missouri. Ameren Missouri, the state's dominant investor-owned utility, and the City of St. Louis were confirmed genuinely blocked earlier in this marathon. This record pivots to Missouri's largest municipal utility and its own independently-governed net metering program instead.

value.name: City Utilities of Springfield
value.notes: Recorded as both the distribution and generation utility.

county.notes: Springfield, Missouri's third-largest city, is the seat of Greene County.

permit_authority.value: City of Springfield Building Development Services

interconnection_url.notes: City Utilities, as a municipal utility, sets its own net metering policy independently of the Missouri Public Service Commission's regulation of investor-owned utilities (Chapter 393, RSMo; 20 CSR 4240-20.065). City Utilities' own page confirms a 100 kW system-size threshold, which happens to match the statewide cap that applies to PSC-regulated IOUs like Ameren Missouri, but City Utilities is not bound by that regulation and sets its terms independently.

battery_programs.notes: No battery storage incentive program was found on City Utilities' or the City of Springfield's own pages this session.

inspection_steps.notes: Neither the City of Springfield's own permits page nor City Utilities' own net metering page published a specific inspection sequence this session — left null rather than guessed.

timeline_days.notes: City Utilities' own net metering page does not publish a specific application review timeline. Missouri's statewide regulation (20 CSR 4240-20.065) sets 30-day (systems 10 kW or less) and 90-day (systems over 10 kW) review windows, but that regulation applies to PSC-regulated investor-owned utilities under Chapter 393, RSMo — City Utilities, as a municipal utility, is not confirmed to be bound by it, so this figure is not attributed to City Utilities specifically.

value.program_or_pathway: City Utilities of Springfield's own net metering program, independently governed by City Utilities rather than the Missouri Public Service Commission. Systems of 100 kW or less use the standard residential net metering application; larger systems use a separate commercial-scale application with a different rate structure.
other_conditions: Excess energy generated flows back onto City Utilities' grid and earns a bill credit at an avoided-cost rate that varies based on system size, rather than necessarily being credited at the full retail rate.

For comparison only (this specific rule applies to PSC-regulated investor-owned utilities like Ameren Missouri, not confirmed to bind City Utilities): Missouri's statewide net metering regulation (20 CSR 4240-20.065) caps net metering at 100 kW, credits excess generation at the utility's filed net metering rate (matching its cogeneration rate), and expires unused credits after 12 months or upon service termination.
